# Overview

To generate a graph, [GitGraph::new()] will read the repository
and assign every commit to a single branch.

It takes the following steps to generate the graph

- Identify branches
- Sort branches by persistence
- Trace branches to commits
- Filtering and indexing

## Identify branches
Local and remote git-branches and tags are used as candidates for branches.
A branch can be identified by a merge commit, even though no current git-branch
refers to it.

## Sort branches by persistence
Each branch is assigned a persistence which can be configured by settings.
Think of persistence as z-order where lower values take preceedence.

## Trace branches to commits
The branches now get to pick their commits, in order of persistence. Each
branch starts with a head, and follow the primary parent while it is
available. It stops when the parent is a commit already assigned to a branch.

## Filtering and indexing

# Branch sorting
The goal of this algorithm is to assign a column number to each tracked branch so that they can be visualized linearly without overlapping in the graph. It uses a shortest-first scheduling strategy (optionally longest-first and with forward/backward start sorting).

## Initialization
- occupied: A vector of vectors of vectors of tuples. 
The outer vector is indexed by the branch's order_group (determined by branch_order based on the settings.branches.order). 
Each inner vector represents a column within that order group, 
and the tuples (start, end) store the range of commits occupied by a branch in that column. 

## Preparing Branches for Sorting
- It creates branches_sort, a vector of tuples containing the branch index, its start commit index (range.0), its end commit index (range.1), its source order group, and its target order group. 
- It filters out branches that don't have a defined range (meaning they weren't associated with any commits). 
## Sorting Branches
- The branches_sort vector is sorted based on a key that prioritizes: 
    1. The maximum of the source and target order groups. This likely aims to keep related branches (e.g., those involved in merges) closer together. 
    2. The length of the branch's lifespan (end - start commit index), either shortest-first or longest-first based on the shortest_first setting. 
    3. The starting commit index, either forward or backward based on the forward setting.

# git-graph manual

**Content**

* [Overview](#overview)
* [Options](#options)
* [Formatting](#formatting)
* [Custom branching models](#custom-branching-models)

## Overview

The most basic usage is to simply call git-graph from inside a Git repository:

```
git-graph
```

This works also deeper down the directory tree, so no need to be in the repository's root folder.

Alternatively, the path to the repository to visualize can be specified with option `--path`:

```
git-graph --path "path/to/repo"
```

**Branching models**

The above call assumes the GitFlow branching model (the default). Different branching models can be used with the option `--model` or `-m`:

```
git-graph --model simple
```

To *permanently* set the branching model for a repository, use subcommand `model`, like

```
git-graph model simple
```

Use the subcommand without argument to view the currently set branching model of a repository:

```
git-graph model
```

To view all available branching models, use option `--list` or `-l` of the subcommand:

```
git-graph model --list
```

For **defining your own models**, see section [Custom branching models](#custom-branching-models).

**Styles**

Git-graph supports different styles. Besides the default `normal` (alias `thin`), supported styles are `round`, `bold`, `double` and `ascii`. Use a style with option `--style` or `-s`:

```
git-graph --style round
```

![styles](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/44003176/103467621-357ce780-4d51-11eb-8ff9-dd7be8b40f84.png)

Style `ascii` can be used for devices and media that do not support Unicode/UTF-8 characters. 

**Formatting**

Git-graph supports predefined as well as custom commit formatting through option `--format`. Available presets follow Git: `oneline` (the default), `short`, `medium` and `full`. For details and custom formatting, see section [Formatting](#formatting).

For a complete list of all available options, see the next section [Options](#options).

## Options

All options are explained in the CLI help. View it with `git-graph -h`:

```
Structured Git graphs for your branching model.
    https://github.com/mlange-42/git-graph

EXAMPES:
    git-graph                   -> Show graph
    git-graph --style round     -> Show graph in a different style
    git-graph --model <model>   -> Show graph using a certain <model>
    git-graph model --list      -> List available branching models
    git-graph model             -> Show repo's current branching models
    git-graph model <model>     -> Permanently set model <model> for this repo

## Custom branching models

Branching models are configured using the files in `APP_DATA/git-graph/models`. 

* Windows: `C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\git-graph`
* Linux: `~/.config/git-graph`
* OSX: `~/Library/Application Support/git-graph`

File names of any `.toml` files in the `models` directory can be used in parameter `--model`, or via sub-command `model`. E.g., to use a branching model defined in `my-model.toml`, use:

```
git-graph --model my-model
```

**Branching model files** are in [TOML](https://toml.io/en/) format and have several sections, relying on Regular Expressions to categorize branches. The listing below shows the `git-flow` model (slightly abbreviated) with explanatory comments.

```toml
# RegEx patterns for branch groups by persistence, from most persistent
# to most short-leved branches. This is used to back-trace branches.
# Branches not matching any pattern are assumed least persistent.
persistence = [
    '^(master|main|trunk)$', # Matches exactly `master` or `main`  or `trunk`
    '^(develop|dev)$',
    '^feature.*$',     # Matches everything starting with `feature`
    '^release.*$',
    '^hotfix.*$',
    '^bugfix.*$',
]

# RegEx patterns for visual ordering of branches, from left to right.
# Here, `master`, `main` or `trunk` are shown left-most, followed by branches
# starting with `hotfix` or `release`, followed by `develop` or `dev`.
# Branches not matching any pattern (e.g. starting with `feature`)
# are displayed further to the right.
order = [
    '^(master|main|trunk)$',      # Matches exactly `master` or `main` or `trunk`
    '^(hotfix|release).*$', # Matches everything starting with `hotfix` or `release`
    '^(develop|dev)$',      # Matches exactly `develop` or `dev`
]

# Colors of branches in terminal output. 
# For supported colors, see section Colors (below this listing).
[terminal_colors]
# Each entry is composed of a RegEx pattern and a list of colors that
# will be used alternating (see e.g. `feature...`).
matches = [
    [
        '^(master|main|trunk)$',
        ['bright_blue'],
    ],
    [
        '^(develop|dev)$',
        ['bright_yellow'],
    ],
    [   # Branches obviously merged in from forks are prefixed with 'fork/'. 
        # The 'fork/' prefix is only available in order and colors, but not in persistence!
        '^(feature|fork/).*$',
        ['bright_magenta', 'bright_cyan'], # Multiple colors for alternating use
    ],
        [
        '^release.*$',
        ['bright_green'],
    ],
        [
        '^(bugfix|hotfix).*$',
        ['bright_red'],
    ],
    [
        '^tags/.*$',
        ['bright_green'],
    ],
]
# A list of colors that are used (alternating) for all branches
# not matching any of the above pattern. 
unknown = ['white']

# Colors of branches in SVG output. 
# Same structure as terminal_colors. 
# For supported colors, see section Colors (below this listing).
[svg_colors]
matches = [
    [
        '^(master|main|trunk)$',
        ['blue'],
    ],
    [ 
        '...',
    ]
]
unknown = ['gray']
```

**Tags**

Internally, all tags start with `tag/`. To match Git tags, use RegEx patterns like `^tags/.*$`. However, only tags that are not on any branch are ordered and colored separately.

**Colors**

**Terminal colors** support the 8 system color names `black`, `red`, `green`, `yellow`, `blue`, `magenta`, `cyan` and `white`, as well as each of them prefixed with `bright_` (e.g. `bright_blue`).

Further, indices of the 256-color palette are supported. For a full list, see [here](https://jonasjacek.github.io/colors/). Indices must be quoted as strings (e.g. `'16'`)

**SVG colors** support all named web colors (full list [here](https://htmlcolorcodes.com/color-names/)), as well as RGB colors in hex notation, like `#ffffff`.

git checkout -q develop; echo b > d1/b.txt; t 02; git add .; git commit -q -m "dev1"

git checkout -q master; t 05; git merge --no-ff -q develop -m "Merge branch 'develop'"
git log --oneline --all --graph --decorate=short
echo "=== graph ==="; /workspace/executable --no-color -d

e8 with a nonstandard message "Merged stuff": only ONE develop entry, no 'm'. So the merge-derived branch isn't created from the message (or the name "unknown" would appear). Interesting: the develop branch still got dev2, dev1.

Hmm, so in e8, there's no merge-derived branch. And the merge commit still draws `○<┐`. So the merge line is drawn because the merge commit has 2 parents, not because of a "merge-derived branch".

So when IS a merge-derived branch created? In t2 ("unknown") and t4. Hmm, in t2 the merge was committed via `git commit` after a conflict — so the merge commit's message was "master2" hmm no wait, in t2 the message was "master2"? Let me recheck t2: I ran `git merge -q --no-ff develop -m "Merge branch 'develop'"` which failed, then `c "master2" "09"` which did `git commit -m "master2"`. So the merge commit's message = "master2". Hmm, and the debug showed "unknown" as the branch that got develop's commits.

Hmm, so in t2 the branch that got dev1..dev3 is named "unknown", and the ref develop entry had col 99 (no commits). So in t2 the merge-derived branch EXISTS and is named "unknown" — but the merge message was "master2" which parses to no branch name → "unknown".

And in t4 (merge message "Merge branch 'develop'"), the merge-derived branch is named "develop" (with 'm' marker) and the ref develop also exists (col 99).

And in e6/e8 (same structure, distinct dates), there's only one develop entry (the ref develop, presumably) with range (1,3).

Hmm, so the merge-derived branch is created in t4 but not e6? Let me compare t4 and e6 super carefully.

t4: commits: merge(0), dev2(1), m1(2), dev1(3), c1(4).
e6: commits: merge(0), dev2(1), B(2), dev1(3), A(4).

Identical structure. Both have merge message "Merge branch 'develop'". Both have develop's tip = dev2.

The ONLY difference is timestamps. So the difference must come from the commit *index ordering*... but they're the same. Hmm, unless in t4 the index order is NOT what I derived!

Let me re-derive t4's index order more carefully using a scenario-based approach. In t4, the ranges: master (0,4), develop (1,3).
- master's chain: merge, m1, c1 (3 commits). Range (0,4) → min=0, max=4.
- develop's chain: dev2, dev1 (2 commits). Range (1,3) → min=1, max=3.

Possible index assignments: merge and c1 get 0 and 4 (in some order). dev2 and dev1 get 1 and 3. m1 gets 2.
Since index 0 = newest? Not necessarily — the index order might not be time-based.

If the index order is: merge=0, dev2=1, m1=2, dev1=3, c1=4 — then rows (in index order) = merge, dev2, m1, dev1, c1. But the rendered rows are merge, m1, dev2, dev1, c1. So rows ≠ index order.

Unless the rendered row order is not index order! Let me re-examine. Hmm, in e6 the rows are merge, dev2, B, dev1, A = index order ✓ (index order = time-desc).

So in e6 rows = index order. In t4 rows ≠ index order (if index order = merge, dev2, m1, dev1, c1).

Alternatively, in t4 rows = index order = merge, m1, dev2, dev1, c1, and the develop range (1,3) means dev2=1? but dev2 is at row 2 → index 2. Contradiction.

So in t4, either rows ≠ index order, or the develop range isn't min/max.

Hmm, so what if the range is NOT min/max but something else that happens to coincide in the distinct-date cases? Let me revisit: maybe the range is (start, end) where start = head index and end = the index of the last row the branch's line passes through (i.e., taken-1 or root).

For e6 develop: dev2(1), dev1(3), branch point A(4). Line from dev2(1) down through dev1(3)... wait, the line spans rows 1,2,3 → end = 3 ✓ (and min/max also gives 3).
For t4 develop: dev2(2), dev1(3) (rows: merge=0, m1=1, dev2=2, dev1=3, c1=4), branch point c1(4) → line spans rows 2..3 → end = 3 ✓ (min/max gives 3 too since dev2=2, dev1=3).
For t4 master: rows merge(0), m1(1), c1(4) → range (0,4) ✓ both.

Hmm, both interpretations agree for t4 under rows=index order. So the discrepancy is in the START: t4 develop start = 1, but under rows=index order, dev2 = 2. So start=1 ≠ dev2's index 2. Hmm! Unless the merge-derived branch's start = the *merge commit's* index? No, that's 0.

Hmm, so under rows=index-order in t4, develop's start = 1 = m1's index. Hmm, m1 = the merge commit's FIRST parent. So the merge-derived branch's range start = merge's first parent index?! And in e6, develop's start = 1 = dev2's index (the second parent). Hmm, in e6 the merge's first parent = B(2).

Hmm, so in t4 develop start = 1 = m1 = first parent; in e6 develop start = 1 = dev2 = second parent. That's inconsistent between interpretations, so one of them is wrong.

Let me settle this by determining t4's index order directly! I can do that by using the commit ordering of the *rows* — but rows ≠ index order (possibly). 

Alternative: use `-n` (max-count) which truncates the commit list. If max-count truncates to the first N indices, I can see which commits survive and infer the index order. Let's do that: t4 with -n 2 shows 2 commits. Let's try.

Actually, better: use `--format "%H"` to see which commits are in which rows, and then compare with -n. Hmm, -n gives the newest N commits presumably. Let's just try -n 1, 2, 3, 4 on t4 and e6 and see which commits appear.

mk(){ rm -rf /tmp/$1 && mkdir /tmp/$1 && cd /tmp/$1 && git init -q .; }
mk e10; for i in 1 2 3 4; do echo $i>f.txt; d "0$i-01" git add .; c "0$i-01" "c$i"; done
git tag v1.0; git tag -a v0.5 4cca670 2>/dev/null || true

echo "=== e10 ==="; /workspace/executable --no-color -d
echo; echo "=== simple model ==="; /workspace/executable --no-color -m simple"}

So the index order in t4 = merge(0), m1(1), dev2(2), dev1(3), c1(4) — matching the rows and `git log --date-order`!

So index order in t4 = merge=0, m1=1, dev2=2, dev1=3, c1=4.

Then develop's range (1,3): develop's chain = dev2(2), dev1(3) → min=2, max=3. But printed (1,3). ✗!!

So the range start is 1 = m1. Hmm! So the merge-derived branch's range starts at the merge commit's FIRST parent index?!

Hmm, but in e6, develop's range (1,3) with index order merge=0, dev2=1, B=2, dev1=3, A=4: develop's chain = dev2(1), dev1(3) → (1,3) ✓ as min/max, and the "first parent" would be B(2). So in e6 the start = 1 = dev2 (second parent), not the first parent.

So t4's develop start = 1 = m1 = first parent, e6's develop start = 1 = dev2 = second parent. Both start at 1 but for different reasons. Hmm, that's a coincidence?!

Unless in t4 the develop branch is NOT the merge-derived one, and the chain is different. Hmm.

Hmm, wait. What if the range's *start* is the index of the *oldest* commit... no, start < end here.

Hmm, what if the range is (start, end) where start = the index of the branch's "tip" in a *filtered* index space? Hmm.

Let me test e6 with -n to double check its index order and range.

Also, let me test more configurations to disentangle. Let me do a cleaner experiment: a merge where the merged branch has 3 commits and master has 3 commits, with distinct dates, and see the merge-derived branch's range (with the 'm' marker appearing only in some cases...).

Hmm, actually, hold on. Let me reconsider the 'm' marker. In t4 the develop entry had 'm' AND t: Some(0). In e6/e8 no 'm' and t: None. What if 'm' + 't: Some(0)' indicates a *merge branch* (created for the merge commit), and the ref develop entry in e6 is the only entry because the merge-derived branch was deduplicated.

In t4, why no dedup? Because... hmm, timestamps.

OK, totally new idea: maybe the branch identification works like this: git-graph looks at each commit in index order. For each commit C that has 2 parents, it creates a "merge branch" whose name is parsed from C's message (or "unknown") and whose head is P2. It also collects refs as branches. THEN, it deduplicates branches that have the same *tip commit*: if a merge branch's tip (P2) equals a ref's tip, they might be merged...

Hmm, in t4 the merge branch's tip = P2 = dev2, and the ref develop's tip = dev2. Same. So dedup should happen.

Unless the dedup compares the branch's *head index* which for the merge branch is set to the merge commit's index? Hmm.

Hmm, let me test a case where P2 is NOT any ref's tip, e.g., delete the branch after merging. That's the "fork" case. Then the merge-derived branch is the only branch for that chain.

Let me also test: merge a branch that is NOT an ancestor chain, e.g., merge develop where develop's tip is P2 and P2 is also the tip of another branch (feature/a). Covered in t3.

Let me try yet another approach to understand the 'm' marker and duplicates: construct a repo where a merge commit's second parent is a commit that is NOT any ref tip, and see the debug.

Also construct: a merge of a branch into master where the merged branch continues after the merge (i.e., the branch tip is newer than P2). Let's see.

git checkout -q master; d "12-01" git merge --no-ff -q feature/a -m "Merge branch 'feature/a'"

In sparse mode, the merge commit's row shows just '○' (no merge arrow), and an extra row is inserted below it: " │<────┐" where the master column has '│' and the merge line starts with '<' at col0's gap.

actions.command:
source /tmp/mk.sh
for n in 1 2 3 4; do
mk r5$n; echo a>a.txt; git add .; c "01-01" "A"
for i in $(seq 1 $n); do git branch feature$i; done
printf "N=%d no-remotes: " $n; /workspace/executable --color always | python3 -c "
import sys,re
l=sys.stdin.read()
print([c for c in re.findall(r'\x1b\[38;5;(\d+)m([^\x1b]*)\x1b\[0m', l) if 'feature' in c[1]])
"
git init -q --bare /tmp/ro5$n.git; git remote add origin /tmp/ro5$n.git; git push -q origin --all >/dev/null 2>&1
printf "N=%d remotes:    " $n; /workspace/executable --color always | python3 -c "
import sys,re
l=sys.stdin.read()
print([c for c in re.findall(r'\x1b\[38;5;(\d+)m([^\x1b]*)\x1b\[0m', l) if 'feature' in c[1]])
"
done

mkc q8; for i in 1 2; do git branch feat$i; done; git tag -m x tv1; git checkout -q feat1; git tag -m x t2; git checkout -q master; cd /tmp/q8 && show q8
